speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the the seventh report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

May we have this report read by the Clerk, Mr. Speaker?
And the Clerk having read the report:

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. My point of order is that this report is not in accordance with the findings of the committee. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the evidence as found in the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 6, of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, for Tuesday, July 29. On page 231 of that report we find this:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall clause 1 carry? We will have a show of hands.
The Clerk: Six in favour, eight against.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we should consider Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 322, which says:
It is not competent for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision, hut if the house resolves that such reconsideration is necessary, the correct procedure is for the house-
House is spelled with a capital letter.
-to give the committee instructions which will enable it to consider the whole question again.
It is my contention, therefore, that you, Mr. Speaker, have one of two alternatives; either you declare this report out of order or you recommit this matter to the committee. There are many references which show this house has the power to recommit a problem to a committee, in which case the committee would then be clear of the decision reached at an earlier meeting.
This morning, Mr. Speaker, the committee met, and without any further ado and despite objections and warnings raised, simply reversed a decision it had made the other day. I should like to call your attention to
citation 325 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. The first paragraph says:
When the report does not contain any resolutions, recommendations or other propositions for consideration of the house, it does not appear that any further proceedings in reference to it as a report are necessary.
I should like to underline the words "are necessary".
Every session, select committees make reports of this description, containing a statement of facts, or of the evidence on the subject of inquiry; but as they do not contain any proposition which can be agreed to by the house, they are simply printed for the information of the members.
The next citation, namely citation 326, I believe is very clear when it says:
326. The report of a standing committee should be considered final only when it is adopted by the house, because, until then, the house can refer it back to the committee with instruction to amend it in any particular.
If you wish other evidence out of Bourinot or May I am willing to produce it, Mr. Speaker. It is for these reasons that I submit that this report should be declared out of order by Your Honour or should be recommitted to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I think a word of explanation here would be in order. The preamble of the bill, which had been carried, reads as follows:
Whereas Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company has by its petition prayed that it be enacted as hereinafter set forth, and it is expedient to grant the prayer of the petition: Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
It has thus been approved in principle. It would have been to negative this action by killing the first clause. There is only one clause in the bill. The feeling of the committee was that there had not been enough discussion. At that time a number of the members put their hands up indicating that they wished the discussion to continue. Also, Mr. Speaker, I understand that if there is any dispute of any kind or disagreement in a standing committee in a case of this kind, the members at that time should have immediately disagreed and asked that it be discussed further or that a vote be taken.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I ask one question of the hon. member who presented the report. Was the report as presented approved by the committee?
3090	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways, Canals, etc.
Mr. Speaker, the report was approved this morning by the committee.

Further to the last point, Mr. Speaker, I should say that the decision of the committee in the first instance is evidenced by the minutes of proceedings and evidence which the chairman did not deny this morning when asked about it. The committee took a vote; it was a vote by count of the clerk, and clause 1 did not carry. However, the hon. member raised the point of immediacy. This is the first time this matter could be raised in this house, Mr. Speaker, as I think you will agree. However, even in the meeting of the committee, when apparently there was some confusion, there is noted at page 231 a comment or a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg South when he said:
Does the vote on clause 1 settle the matter or is it to go on indefinitely?
I contend that he answered himself when he said "or is it to go on indefinitely?" Definitely, according to the rules whereby a committee may not reverse its decision, it would have to go on indefinitely, for the meeting to continue. Then, following that, the hon. member for Winnipeg South said, "We should now adjourn." There appeared to have been a number of members of the committee who understood at that time that the matter had been settled and the bill had been defeated in committee. However, the chairman said, "I asked our clerk if we could go on and he said yes."
The hon. member for Peterborough now makes the point that the preamble was endorsed. From all my reading of the rules, when you endorse the preamble you have satisfied yourself that all the conditions necessary for the consideration of the bill have been met; that is the endorsation of the preamble. I have always taken it, and have so been advised by others, that clause 1, which in this case is the one and only clause and the operative clause, is in effect the principle of the bill. The preamble only assures to us that it is right and proper that the committee do now consider amending a certain act at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order may be in effect an appeal from the chairman's ruling. Perhaps the best course to follow, as this is not a matter of immediate urgency, would be to allow me to consider the point of order which has been raised and to hold the item, which would normally go to the committee of the whole, until it has been disposed of.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker; and while you are considering it would you also consider the gross discrepancy which 

appears as between the evidence on page 231, recording this vote, and the minutes which say at one stage that the chairman asked whether the clause would carry and, "on a show of hands the committee decided to continue the discussion".

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if when you are considering this matter you could also consider the point that the vote on page 231 of the report was, in my contention, a nullity. 1 would refer you to page 354 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, where it says:
All questions before committees on private bills are decided by a majority of voices including the voice of the chairman; and whenever the voices are equal, the chairman has a second or casting vote.
Then under citation 491 on the same page it continues:
491. (1) The names of the members attending each committee are entered by the committee clerk in the minutes; and when a division takes place, the clerk takes down the names of the members, distinguishing on which side of the question they respectively vote; and such lists are to be given in, with the report, to the house.
There was merely a show of hands vote, Your Honour. Accordingly it is my contention that the vote was a nullity and that therefore we were in order in carrying on the meeting.
The second vote was exactly the same.

And in addition, Your Honour, the matter was referred to the committee and I think that is the place where the appeal should be made; and I know Beauchesne does refer to that as the proper practice rather than appealing to the house. The committee unanimously decided that it was correct.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will take the matter under consideration. It may be that it should be disposed of in the committee itself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Having just studied Hansard, Mr. Speaker, I think it is correct to say that no question was asked yesterday with regard to an alleged discussion between a representative of the Southam Press and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and it is that particular discussion which has been reported in the press about which I am inquiring.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, this whole question was canvassed at considerable length yesterday and it developed into what was nothing more than a cross-examination or a fishing expedition.

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext:
Today the Leader of the Opposition comes into the house with a similar question in which he refers by name to a member of the press gallery, and he wants to conduct a further cross-examination in regard to this particular member of the gallery. If the hon. member can do that he can do the same thing with regard to every individual member of the press gallery. I submit that questions of this type are entirely out of order when we are considering orders of the day.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, a report has appeared in more than one newspaper in Canada under the byline of Mr. Bruce Phillips of Ottawa commenting on a conversation which he had with the Minister of Trade and Commerce on this particular matter, which is of very considerable importance, and this particular interview was not referred to by the minister.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext:
May I say to the Leader of the Opposition that what I am concerned about is the propriety of the question, not the circumstances which gave rise to it. We did have an extended inquiry of the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday as to his conversations with various members of the press, and as the matter was in the course of his public responsibilities I allowed the question and a number of supplementary questions.
If the hon. member's question today is a new inquiry about a new situation or involving circumstances which were not inquired about yesterday, I would be disposed to permit it, but I am not disposed to allow the minister to be cross-examined by a great many supplementary questions. We are in the middle of a debate involving this whole matter, and it seems to me that hon. members will be able to air their views sufficiently there. It is only a search for limited information which can be permitted.
In so far as the question relates to the use of the word "violent" I rule it out of order, but I am disposed to let the other part of the question stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Perhaps I could rephrase my question in this form. Is the statement made in the Hamilton Spectator of August 2 and attributed to the minister, to the effect that he was conducting or had ordered to be conducted an investigation into the leakage of the report "The Canadian Economic Outlook, 1958", accurate?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Before the minister answers that question, may I say that I do not think a question of that type is permissible. If the hon. member will refer to Beauchesne he will find that he states quite positively that a question simply directed to the verification of a statement in the press is not in order. If the hon. member wished to ask the minister whether he had a conversation with the gentleman in question I would consider that a proper question, but not the one that he put.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Thank you for your suggestion, Mr. Speaker. I will now ask the minister whether he had a telephone conversation with Mr. Bruce Phillips of the Southam Press regarding this alleged leakage and an investigation that was being conducted into it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was Mr. Bruce Phillips who, as I recollect, first informed me that there would be a story appearing in the Toronto Star.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: You knew about it.

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Make what you can of that.

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, since he admitted last night that the extracts in the Toronto Star were based on "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958", if the government will now table that document?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Order. I think that question involves a subject before the house in debate at the moment, and the hon. member might defer his question until the debate is completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: May I also point out on a point of order that the hon. member has quite improperly smuggled into what purports to be a question something which he alleges to be a statement of fact and which is not a statement of fact, never was and I think never will be.

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: I assume, Mr. Speaker, since the minister has raised a point of order, that you will hear me briefly on it. One was the budget speech, and the minister took no exception to the quotations from the budget speech-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Who says that?

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: -so it is perfectly obvious that the statements that were distorted beyond recognition were from "The Canadian Economic Outlook". You cannot distort something you have not seen.

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN

maintopic: CANADIAN ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 1958"- INQUIRY AS TO TELEPHONE DISCUSSION WITH NEWSPAPERMAN

Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I realize that the Chicago water steal is an old threat to the welfare of great lakes communities, but it has new urgency now because of the water needs of the St. Lawrence seaway and Niagara power. The increased diversion of lake Michigan water for Chicago sewage purposes will raise the cost of Niagara power and endanger the St. Lawrence seaway. speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smiih (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: APPLICATION BY SONS OF FREEDOM TO EMIGRATE TO RUSSIA
speechtext: I wonder whether I could put a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has the government received any application from the sons of freedom or any group of the sons of freedom for financial assistance to emigrate to Russia?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPLICATION BY SONS OF FREEDOM TO EMIGRATE TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would permit me to answer that question. News reports have been brought to my attention in which it is said that a statement has been issued

on behalf of the sons of freedom sect of the Doukhobors that they wish to return to Russia provided certain conditions are agreed to by governments, from which I take it they mean the government of British Columbia and the government of Canada.
I have not actually seen an authentic copy of the statement purported to have been made, but since the matter may be related to discussions which have been taking place between this government and the government of British Columbia concerning a solution of the Doukhobor problem, and in which I have taken part, I have communicated with the premier of the province indicating that it would be desirable if he could let us have his views and let us have an indication as to what the government of British Columbia desires to do with respect to the specific solution of the problem which has been under discussion between us.

I be permitted to ask the Prime Minister a question. What is the present position of the proposed summit meeting?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, the only information that is available today is contained in a message received by the President of the United States from Mr. Khrushchev, in which Mr. Khrushchev asks that an extraordinary meeting of the United Nations assembly be convened, and I think the wording is, for the purpose of considering the question of the withdrawal of United States troops from Lebanon and British troops from Jordan. He is asking for an extraordinary meeting, and has obviously changed his attitude in the last few days or certainly in the last two weeks.
I have no observations to make on this change, with the exception that it has all the appearances that, Mr. Khrushchev having himself been faced with the reference of the summit meeting to the security council which was available to him, is now seeking means to delay the meeting of the security council which was proposed with a view to alleviating the situation in the Middle East. It is a change of front on his part, and one that indicates a great detour from the course he has been requesting for the last several weeks.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Last evening, Mr. Speaker, I had dealt in an introductory way with some of the corrections of which the Leader of the Opposition plainly indicated he needed to be reminded in relation to the budget speech. I had, I know, disappointed him by not being gloomy. Indeed, the whole burden of the complaint of the Leader of the Opposition was that the budget speech was not pessimistic enough; and to establish his case, such as it was, he proceeded to wrench out of context things that were said in the budget speech, and to ignore completely many things that have to be taken into account in gauging the whole tenor of the speech.
The hon. gentleman has had a good deal to say about quotations and about excerpts. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is notable that in dealing with the budget speech last night, and in all his references to it, the Leader of the Opposition did not make one direct quotation. If he is going to make references I should think when the record is plain for all to read the least that might be expected of him under such circumstances, when he is making the kind of complaint he is, is that he should make direct quotations. It is interesting, also, that in his selection of excerpts from the budget speech he did not follow any consecutive course. The selection and sequence of the excerpts taken from the budget speech are to be found in the Toronto Daily Star.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: How do you know; you said you had not read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: The hon. member opposite will sometime or other perhaps, Mr. Speaker, understand the meaning of plain language, but as yet he has given no indication of being able to do so.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: May I address a question to the minister; I am rising on a question of privilege. The minister has called my accuracy into question. I ask him if he did not tell us yesterday he had not read the item in the Toronto Star?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I have taken careful note, Mr. Speaker, of the references to the budget speech in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition. I am going to

Canadian Economic Outlook deal with them in relation to the quotations ascribed to the budget speech in the Toronto Daily Star.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That does not answer my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Nobody could
answer such an utterly foolish and childish question.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: It is quite simple; did you read it or did you not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition chose to make four references to the budget speech. I note, Mr. Speaker, in the references to the article to which he directed our attention in his speech last evening, that the excerpts he has referred to are those appearing in the Toronto Daily Star, and in that order. He did not even have enough originality to change the order. He did not have enough originality to turn to the budget speech itself. Apparently it is enough that reference is made in the Toronto Daily Star, so he starts from there.
I should like to say a word or two about those references to the budget speech. The first reference in which the Leader of the Opposition indulged is found on page 3076 of Hansard for August 4, 1958. This is an accurate one, because here he departed from the language of the Toronto Daily Star-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Which you did not read.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
-and which I have had an opportunity of checking against the references to it by the hon. gentleman in his remarks last night. First he talked about my reference to the rapidly narrowing gap in the percentage of unemployed as compared with a year ago. Yes, the Leader of the Opposition was correct in that reference, but the Toronto Daily Star was not.
He referred farther down on page 3076, Mr. Speaker, to a statement I had made, and which appears on page 1235 of the budget speech, where I said that "there are hopeful signs that we have reached the end of the recent decline". The Leader of the Opposition correctly quoted that one.
The next one, however, provides an interesting contrast. This is the third reference of the Leader of the Opposition to the budget speech. Here his remarks are in rather striking contrast to those appearing in the Toronto Daily Star, which was his guide. What I said is, I think, not to be confused with what the Toronto Daily Star has said on this subject as attributed to the budget speech. What the Toronto Daily Star has said-and this will be a fair guide, I think, by which to test the accuracy of this article-is this:

Mr. Fleming forecast the 1958 gross national product-the value of goods and services produced -would be up two per cent over 1957, or $32 million.
What I said, Mr. Speaker, and this will be found at page 1235 of Hansard, is:
Assuming normal crops, stable prices and no untoward external events, I am basing my revenue forecasts on a gross national product of $32 billion, which is about 2 per cent above the level achieved in 1957.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is exactly what is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate says, "That is exactly what is here." "Here" must mean somewhere in the recesses of his mind, because it is not what the Toronto Daily Star said. You see, what the Toronto Daily Star did was to omit entirely the governing words where I said:
Assuming normal crops, stable prices and no untoward external events-
This is interesting, Mr. Speaker. I suppose one should not expect too much in the way of accuracy from the Toronto Daily Star, Mr. Speaker, but you will notice that the Toronto Daily Star says that a 2 per cent increase over 1957 is $32 million. It says:
-would be up two per cent over 1957, or $32 million.
What I said was that I was basing my revenue forecast on a gross national product of $32 billion, but apparently the difference between millions and billions makes little impression upon the mind of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I am drawing attention to the fact that the Leader of the Opposition has followed slavishly the selections from the Toronto Daily Star, and he has asked the house and the country to believe that the inferences which that paper seeks to draw with respect to the budget speech are correct when you see the sort of inaccuracies that appear in them now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order. The minister is challenging the accuracy of what I have said in relation to his budget speech and is basing his own remarks on something I am supposed to have said about the Toronto Star.
Perhaps I had better read exactly what I did say. It is to be found at page 3076 of Hansard. This is what I said, and I commend it to my hon. friend.
The Minister of Finance said, and I am sure he will remember this portion of his budget speech, that assuming normal crops, stable prices and no untoward external events he was basing his revenue

forecasts on a gross national product of $32 billion which is about 2 per cent above the level achieved in 1957.
There is no mention of the Toronto Daily Star in connection with that statement at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Reference to the Toronto Daily Star ran all through the Leader of the Opposition's speech and was the whole basis of his selections. The whole sequence of his speech was based on the Toronto Daily Star.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Be honest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
That is a point which is perfectly plain and unchallengeable on the part of the Leader of the Opposition. I am going to have something to say a little later about the nature of the emphasis of the Leader of the Opposition.
What is the basis of the budget forecast? Mr. Speaker, the basis of the budget forecast appearing in the budget speech of June 17 was advice based on conditions existing right up to the time of delivery of the budget speech. It was not based upon reviews of conditions in January. It was not based upon reviews of conditions in February. It was not based upon reviews of conditions in March. It was not based upon reviews of conditions in April. It was not based upon reviews of conditions in May. It was based upon-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Speculation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
-the most up to date indicators at the date of the delivery of the budget on June 17. When hon. gentlemen opposite want to restrict the government in its consideration of what are sound and reliable economic indicators to situations long before the budget date, I wish to tell the opposition-and I know it will bring them no joy-that the Canadian economy in the early days of this spring had showed very great strength. It was in the light of the conditions of strength that were shown in the Canadian economy in the spring right up until June 17, when the budget speech was delivered, that the budget was based upon those conditions and an up to the minute review of them.
That was the basis of the budget indications. That was the basis of the budget speech. Timing apparently means nothing to hon. gentlemen opposite as long as they can live in and create an atmosphere of gloom. These gloom mongers are doing no service to Canada. The strength of the Canadian economy shown this spring was a matter that brought no joy to members of the opposition. The strength which the economy showed served to abate a great deal of the uncertainty that had existed in earlier months, and to impart to
Canadian Economic Outlook the whole of Canadian business and Canadian activities of all kinds a more confident tone than had existed. Mr. Speaker, it was on this basis, the basis of the latest economic indicators with the best advice available in Canada to a minister of finance, that this budget was based and all its forecasts.
I took the responsibility with my colleagues of weighing those up to the minute indicators. I accepted them. I believed them. On them I based this budget. Those economic facts are there in the white paper for all to read, for all who will take the trouble to read; but we have not seen much indication on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite that they have taken the trouble to peruse the incontestable facts appearing in the white paper.
I have this further to say, Mr. Speaker. If there are any persons who might seek to indulge in the baseless suggestion that the Canadian people were not led along factual bases in the budget forecast in appraising the economic forces at work in Canada at the time, may I say that no such complaint lies in the mouth of hon. gentlemen opposite. They cannot complain that there was any misleading because they, in their budget speeches, showed that they took a divergent attitude.
I took the trouble yesterday to look up the record and to see again what the Leader of the Opposition himself had to say in his own speech on the budget. It will be found in Hansard of July 3, and I am referring particularly to pages 1902 and 1903. This is from a member of this house who now undertakes to say that there were divergences between the budget forecast and something else, and says evidently that he thinks the something else was sound and the budget forecast was wrong. This is supposed to be something new. The hon. gentleman would have the house and the country believe that he has found something new. It is a very old story, Mr. Speaker. It is a month old. It is stale in the mouth of the Leader of the Opposition. Here is what he said in his own speech on the budget, as reported at page 1902 of Hansard:
-I am quite sure that any observations I am going to make will result in my being accused of spreading doom and gloom-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Precisely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Precisely; that is
correct. That is exactly the line the hon. gentleman followed then and is following now. He was not satisfied with the budget prediction that we were going to have a budget deficit this year of $648 million. He was going to improve on it. So he said the deficit will likely be over $1 billion. Those are his words as found at page 1902 of

Canadian Economic Outlook Hansard. Can anybody who said that a month ago complain that he was misled by the budget forecast?
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, he talked yesterday about the gross national product and my forecast of a gross national product for this year of 1958 of $32 billion, on three given assumptions. But the hon. gentleman had this to say as reported at page 1902 of Hansard of July 3. Speaking of what he called the optimistic deficit figure, he said this:
-it is based on a forecast of a gross national product of $32 billion which is, as I have said, a 2 per cent increase, assuming there is no significant rise in prices and assuming normal crops. After what we have heard this afternoon about the situation in the west, that is a somewhat risky assumption to make.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, that on July 3 the Leader of the Opposition was a little hesitant about building any case on assumptions, but when August 4 came along he was so desperate, he was so hard put to it for something to say on the final supply motion of this session, that he based his whole case on the riskiest kinds of assumptions and on nothing else. Then his remarks continue:
However, that is his assumption.
There he refers to the assumption of the Minister of Finance, and then he continues:
He also leads us to believe that he is basing that estimate on the 1958 investment outlook, this assumption of a 2 per cent increase.
Then the hon. gentleman dwells on the subject of the gross national product and he continues, as recorded further down the page:

and it seems to me difficult to understand how the minister can reconcile a 2 per cent increase in our gross national product with a 3 per cent decrease in total capital outlay without any price rise and with agricultural prices remaining normal.
He proceeded later on, after his review, to sum it up in these words:
[DOT]-which justified, I think, our caution in this regard.
Then he went on to say the following:
That figure-
The figure he referred to was the figure on the gross national product of Canada published by the dominion bureau of statistics, and listen to this, Mr. Speaker, if you will, in relation to a man and coming from the mouth of a man who is an hon. member of this house who has said there is something hidden which this house ought to have:
The most recent piece of evidence we have-and the minister must surely be acquainted with it- is the figure published by the dominion bureau of statistics on the gross national product for the first quarter of 1958. That figure is $31.7 billion which, seasonally adjusted at annual rates, shows
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).J

an increase of only 0.7 per cent over the comparable adjusted figure for the last quarter of 1957.
Yet in his speech yesterday the Leader of the Opposition tried to raise a hue and cry by saying that the gross national product estimated by the Minister of Finance at $32 billion with an increase of 2 per cent over 1957 had misled the country, because some other source had said the increase was going to be only 0.7 per cent. This was a brand new discovery. The Minister of Finance had misled the country because he had not given the figure of 0.7 per cent. One month ago the same figure of 0.7 per cent was put on record before the final vote was taken, and before the house resolved itself into committee of ways and means on the budget resolutions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: From a different source.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: This was something which was put before the house. The 0.7 per cent was based upon a government record issued by the dominion bureau of statistics.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Whose estimates were better than yours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
This just illustrates how really silly and misleading was the case which the Leader of the Opposition tried to make out in this house last night. It was misleading because he tried to make it appear that something had been hidden; he tried to make it appear that he had discovered something new, something which the government should be called upon to answer. Mr. Speaker, this was answered in the course of the budget debate; this was all put before the house, and the house passed its judgment on that kind of statement on that very night in question, July 3, following the speech of the Leader of the Opposition.
Therefore let there be an end to this kind of hollow pretence, to this sham play on the part of the Leader of the Opposition. He talked last night about hypocrisy, which he attributed to a right hon. member of this house, but I would say to him that he is the last person in this house, in view of his performance last night, who should be talking about hypocrisy on the part of any other hon. member.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member has accused me of hypocrisy on the basis that I used a figure in my budget debate speech from a report which indicated that the increase in the gross national product had been merely 0.7 per cent, and therefore, having said last night that this report had been hidden, I had been

hypocritical. The report I was talking about, or the excerpts from the report to which I referred last night, was an entirely different report from that from the Department of Trade and Commerce, which had no relationship whatsoever to the first report. It happened, however, to come to the same conclusion as this Department of Trade and Commerce report, namely that the increase was 0.7 per cent. These are two separate and distinct reports and one had no relation to the other, which the minister of course knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I think it is not amiss for me to point out that in speaking as he did last night the Leader of the Opposition, unless he has completely forgotten the facts and unless he has completely forgotten his own argument on July 3, could not have failed to mislead the house if he had succeeded in making the house believe that there was something new, something hidden, something heinous about there having been no disclosure of the figure of 0.7 per cent. The dominion bureau of statistics put out that figure and the Leader of the Opposition was aware of it and put it on the record in this house away back on July 3. If what has been said by the Leader of the Opposition was not hypocrisy, then I think the hon. gentleman will have to amend his conceptions and his definitions.
Something was said by the Leader of the Opposition last night about unemployment figures and forecasts, as though we had asked the house to believe that unemployment in Canada was going to follow some figure we had put before the house. In the budget speech I did not put a figure before the house as to what unemployment was going to be. There cannot be any suggestion that this house was misled by any figure given; far from it. But listen, Mr. Speaker, to what the Leader of the Opposition said on this subject on July 3 and match it with that bogus display we witnessed here last night, when he tried to make it appear that the country had been misled and that unemployment is going to be even more severe this year than indicated in the budget forecast. Did he accept the estimate in the forecast? This is what the hon. gentleman had to say as recorded at page 1902:
Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for us to accept this optimistic conclusion of the minister because the evidence seems to us to point in the other direction, and if that is the case surely the minister should be taking this into consideration in the plans and policies which he must be preparing at the present time.
But even if we assumed an increase of 2 per cent in gross national product in 1958, what would be the employment outlook for the current year? The hon. member for Essex East-
Canadian Economic Outlook
And we know that hon. member is probably the least reliable guesser on the extent of unemployment in Canada-
-made his projection this afternoon, and I think, without going into the details he went into, that if there is this 2 per cent increase in the gross national product and if there is the same ratio between that figure and employment which has existed over recent years, it would mean we would have an increase of about 1 per cent in employment in this country in 1958 as compared with 1957. If there is an addition to the labour force of 2.5 per cent we would have considerably more unemployment next year than last year, and the peak figure would be far too high. I am willing to leave it at that.
The Leader of the Opposition last night tried to make it appear that the house had been misled by statements and forecasts appearing in the budget speech. These are his own words before the close of his budget speech. He challenged these budget forecasts, so how can he now pretend, even to himself, that there was anything in this budget speech by which anyone was misled? He dismissed that subject with a passing reference to the mathematics of the hon. member for Essex East and this additional sentence:
The implications with regard to unemployment are serious, but the implications with regard to inflation are just as serious.
The hon. gentleman then went on to deal with the dangers of inflation in, I think, somewhat the same terms as I had dealt with them in my budget speech, and all this adds up to is this-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, are we debating the budget all over again or are we debating an amendment of my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is not an easy question to answer. The amendment which was moved at the end of the address by the Leader of the Opposition was much more restrictive in character than the Leader of the Opposition's own remarks, and in his address he dealt with much the same subject matter as the Minister of Finance is dealing with, so I do not think I should restrict him in his reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I complete this portion of my remarks with the conclusion that there can be no complaint from hon. gentlemen opposite that they were misled by anything in the budget forecast, because it is plainly apparent from their own remarks that they did not accept them and that they disagreed then with the budget forecast.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
But the public was misled.

Canadian Economic Outlook

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
And there is no shadow of substance in their statement now that something has been discovered today, or within the last four or five days, which throws doubt on the budget forecast. They threw every possible doubt on those budget forecasts before the conclusion of the budget debate, and the house has passed its judgment on those doubts in the decision that was taken in the vote on July 3.
It was on the basis of remarks like these that the Leader of the Opposition last night proceeded to draw some extraordinary conclusions as to the way in which he alleged the whole fabric of government had been shaken. At page 3075 of Hansard he undertook to say that "economic forecasting by officials in Canada, to which Canadian governments have become accustomed and upon which they have come to rely, has now for all practical purposes been weakened and prejudiced".
By what authority does the Leader of the Opposition make a statement of that kind? I say to him that that statement has not one single tittle or scintilla of truth in it. Nothing has been prejudiced in the relations between the government's officers in the civil service and the government. But the hon. gentleman last night did everything that lay within his power to create that kind of condition between the government and the civil service of which he complained. If there is anything that is prejudiced in this debate or in public discussion of recent days in relation to the position of the civil servants in this matter it is attributable to, and lies at the doorstep of, the Leader of the Opposition. Nothing has happened to come between the government and its advisers in the civil service, and to suggest that there has been some prejudice created by the course of action of the government is to deny the facts and to substitute for facts something that is really not true.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question. Is it not true that since January 20 the deputy minister of trade and commerce has resigned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should not have thought the hon. gentleman would have sought to make political capital by descending to that kind of remark in a situation of this sort. The deputy minister of trade and commerce exercised the right of any member of the civil service to resign in order to take up a position outside the civil service. Did no deputy minister resign during the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite? Of course they did.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Not under those circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: What circumstances is the hon. member for Laurier talking about?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: If I get an opportunity to speak this afternoon I will indicate to you in what circumstances.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You just stop talking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition is endeavouring to enforce closure-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: But we have no flag.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I do not believe I am subject to his command with regard to the speech I make. I did not pretend in the first place that what I was going to say was going to please him, and if he expects that the balance of my remarks are intended to have that effect let me disabuse his mind at once. The Leader of the Opposition finished up last night, before he proceeded to give birth to this misshapen amendment, by summarizing his conclusion in the following words at page 3077 of Hansard-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Talk it out, Don.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I am sure that no amount of talk or intelligence around here would be able to pierce the outer covering of the hon. member's cranium.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: May I suggest to the house that there are too many collateral debates going on. If hon. members would not interrupt, and if the hon. member who has the floor would not pay any attention to interruptions, we could get on faster.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: This was the conclusion reached by the Leader of the Opposition last night as reported at page 3077 of Hansard; "The entire system of economic reporting has now been prejudiced. That, Mr. Speaker, is the main burden of our attack on the government in this matter".

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Those were heroic words, Mr. Speaker, but there is not a word of truth in them. six weeks ago but, Mr. Speaker, we believe that it it was given again now it would be in almost identical terms.

The true test of this budget forecast is, I am sure, going to be the test of time itself. That will be the test, taking due account of all the factors which enter into the budget speech and the budget forecasts. I am going to ask the house simply to consider what has happened in this respect since the 17th day of June. Let the house measure the accuracy of the budget forecasts by what has happened at any rate since the 17th day of June, when the budget was delivered. Here let me be brief. Let us take a few of the more important economic indicators of interest to all Canadians.
On July 31 the crop year closed in Canada. Our marketings of wheat in this country are of tremendous importance to the wellbeing of the whole Canadian economy. In the crop year ended July 31, 1958, Canada's exports of wheat totalled 312 million bushels. The export figure for the previous year, the crop year ended July 31, 1957, was 50 million bushels less than the total exported during *this most recent crop year.

The Leader of the Opposition last night, referring to the budget speech, had something to say as well about the cost of living, as found at page 3077. He chose to make reference to the Toronto Daily Star, and he said I had said that the cost of living would remain stable. Let us look at what I said and then let us examine

Canadian Economic Outlook
the facts. In the budget speech on June 17 as recorded at page 1234 of Hansard I said:
In the absence of immediate inflationary pressures I would not expect any general increase in prices during the balance of 1958. But this is not something we can take for granted.
You see, Mr. Speaker, this is the part the Leader of the Opposition completely omitted and glossed over. I continue:
But this is not something we can take for granted. It is the duty of all groups and classes in our society to ensure that the prospects for a sound recovery are not dimmed by a spiralling of costs or that efforts to stimulate recovery do not lend strength to a new inflation. Inflation remains a very real danger against which we must remain on guard.
What are the facts since the 17th day of June? Between May and June the consumer price index in this country remained unchanged, and between June and July the consumer price index in this country dropped four tenths of a point from 125.1 to 124.7. Is the government to be condemned on that score?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
No. And as for the
wholesale price index, Mr. Speaker, if the Leader of the Opposition will refer to the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics for July 4 he will find there that the wholesale price index has dropped also.
But we attach great importance in this country to the volume of our exports. What is the record of exports from this country since June 17? In the first half of the year 1958 Canada's exports reached an all-time record for the first half of any year, an all-time record. Does this sound like leading the Canadian people to accept an altogether too optimistic view of Canada's prospects when we budgeted on the basis of an increase of 2 per cent in the gross national product? Exports of Canadian goods in the first six months of 1958 were valued at $2,338 million, 2.2 per cent higher than in the corresponding period of 1957.
In weighing the extent of this increase it is well to bear in mind that the increase in the second quarter of 1958 grew faster than in the first quarter. In the second quarter of 1958 Canadian exports increased by about 7 per cent in value compared to that quarter of 1957 and thus went up at a sharper rate than in the first six months as a whole. I think those are significant statistics.
I do not say, however, that everything has gone up. Here is the index of industrial production. The latest figure is for May 1958. The seasonally adjusted figures on the basis that the period from 1935 to 1939 equals 100 are as follows: The figure for May, 1958 was

278.7 as compared with a figure in January, 1958 of 275.8 and a figure in May, 1957 of 286.7. Labour income seasonally adjusted and expressed in millions of dollars showed the following figures. The latest figure is for April, 1958, $1,304 million. In January, 1958 it was $1,283 million. In April, 1957 it was $1,263 million.
Let us examine the average hours worked per week in manufacturing, seasonally adjusted. The figures are as follows: May, 1958, 40.3; January, 1958, 39.5; May, 1957, 40.6. With respect to manufacturers' shipments in Canada the figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics on July 10 show that in the first five months of 1958 our figure was within 3 per cent of the figure in the same period of 1957.
Let us look at housing, Mr. Speaker. The figures on housing construction in Canada, for those who are prepared to take a realistic and not just a pessimistic, gloomy view like hon. members opposite, are indeed gratifying. The outlook is for the construction in Canada in 1958 of a record total of 150,000 housing units. The previous record was in 1955, 138,000 units. In 1956 there were 127,000 units and in 1957, 122,000 units.
In June, when there was a marked increase in employment in Canada, a strong advance occurred in forestry and construction. It accounted for about 60 per cent of the employment gain. Construction employment reached almost 500,000, about 30,000 higher than a year earlier. The recovery in the housing industry has been largely stimulated by a record-breaking house building program. The year to year increase in new housing units started was smaller in June than in preceding months. The six-month total, however, is 66 per cent higher than the comparable 1957 figure. I am sure these figures are much too favourable to bring any comfort to hon. gentlemen opposite.
There is a very interesting report in this morning's issue of the Montreal Gazette which reads as follows.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Page 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
It is headed "Construction at Record High, Up 21.2 Per Cent in first seven months". The first paragraph in this article reads as follows:
Another record has been established by Canada's surging construction industry. For the first time the total cumulative dollar volume of construction contract awards for the first seven months has passed the $2 billion mark.
Figures based on information collected by Hugh C. MacLean Building Reports show that the 1958 seven-month cumulative total is $2,000,887,900. This is an increase of $360,672,400 or 21.2 per cent over the same period in 1957, and $5,295,800 above the

figure for 1956, the previous record year. This trend in dollar volume has now been maintained for the past four months of 1958.
These are figures which I am sure will bring satisfaction to all Canadians who do not take a jaundiced, political, partisan view of their country's outlook. They will not, of course, bring comfort to hon. members opposite. This gratifying increase points to a record construction program which will ensure a high level of employment in both the construction industry and in the industries supplying building materials.
The function of the administration in reference to the National Housing Act is worthy of comment. N.H.A. loan requests received during the first 30 weeks of 1958 compared with 1957 are as follows: 1957, the first 30 weeks, 15,562, and the first 30 weeks of 1958, 28,264. Yet we are asked to believe that the outlook for Canadians is gloomy.
One could go on, Mr. Speaker. I think I might make mention of the latest employment figures. The latest figures are those as of June 21 issued on July 21. These are the official figures compiled jointly by the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics. They show that on June 21 the number of Canadians who had jobs was 5,794,000. That figure was an increase of 129,000 over the figure for one month earlier and it is only 40,000 less than the figure of one year earlier.
These are significant figures, Mr. Speaker. They are not to be brushed aside after the fashion of hon. members opposite. If they had referred to the actual release to which I have referred they would have seen that the estimated number of persons without jobs and seeking employment decreased by 46,000 during the month to 320,000, representing 5.2 per cent of the labour force compared with 2.7 per cent a year earlier. The number of persons with jobs who were laid off for the full week declined another 4,000 to 15,000. These figures indicating the decrease in unemployment are, I think, figures that fully bear out what I had to say in the budget speech when I said, as found on page 1233:
Once again the latest figures are encouraging, showing a rapidly narrowing gap in the percentage of unemployed as compared with a year ago.
On June 21 the gap was down to 40,000 out of a total labour force of approximately six million.
So, Mr. Speaker, the government is quite prepared to stand by the budget. The government is quite prepared to stand by the forecasts upon which the budget was based. The government takes its responsibility in doing so. The government had access to the best and very latest advice in the country available at that date.
Canadian Economic Outlook
The budget was not born in an attitude of black pessimism. It was not born, on the other hand, of any Pollyanna attitude of disregarding the existence of facts in the economy that are unfavourable. The budget was based upon a realistic and factual appraisal of all of the factors at work in the Canadian economy at June 17, whether favourable or unfavourable, and that basis of budget writing has not been called into question by anything that has been said in the house by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). In writing budgets we do not intend to follow the example of hon. gentlemen opposite who glory in gloom and who are unhappy in the face of the strength of the Canadian economy.
We witnessed a demagogic display last evening on the part of the Leader of the Opposition put on for what were thought to be the partisan interests of the official opposition. Evidently it did not matter to him that he might in the course of his irresponsible remarks be doing damage to Canada's credit or shaking confidence on the part of Canadians, if there are any who pay any attention to anything that the Leader of the Opposition says. After what he said last night it is perfectly clear to all Canadians that the opposition does not want improvement in economic conditions in Canada. What they want is a condition of affairs under which they can derive some partisan advantage, and so if there is not room for gloom, if there is not occasion for gloom, they are not going to be happy unless they create gloom.

Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in the Toronto Star story to indicate what report of the various reports that I receive was being referred to.

The trade and commerce department's hitherto secret report on Canada's 1958 economic prospects-

The report-which the government has consistently refused to table in the House of Commons-

-Is normally one of the main factors upon which the finance minister bases his budget calculations.
