Mr. Speaker, I had thought that we were talking about this hidden report, but the minister has warmed over his budget speech, he has made a lot of extravagant statements today as he did yesterday, many of which he made in his budget speech. He made one statement which was not extravagant and which is correct, namely that Canada s exports of wheat have gone up by 50 million bushels. I asked him about the price and he said it was the highest price in the world; when I questioned him further he said, "The highest price in a free market". Why is it lower than the Chicago market price by 20 cents? I have in my hand the most recent edition of the international federation of agricultural producers publication, the IFAP News, which reports the prices of wheat paid in eighteen countries, and I see that Canada has the distinction of paying the lowest price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend realizes we are talking about wheat in the export markets.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I said that the farmers were getting the lowest price since the end of the war. The minister has said it is the highest price in a free market, which is not true; that just is not true. The prices start with Canada having the lowest price of $1.40 per bushel, the United Kingdom $1.50, just 10 cents more, Argentina, $1.52, Australia, $1.63, and so on, up and up and up, until you come to Turkey with a price of $4.46 per bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: What are you talking about?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The nub of what we are discussing and the thing which I think bothers Canadians most at this time is that this

government is now prepared to hide a report which it accused the former government of having hidden. Although this government used a roundabout and tortuous way of gaining votes on March 31-which they did gain-now, when they are faced with identical circumstances they run away and they are not consistent. They will not disclose this report, but for the Canadian people one of the most interesting and important aspects of the matter is that when the Liberal government was advised that we were in for tough times and that unemployment would rise, they did little or nothing. When the same group of economic advisers in the same government department advised this government that we were in for tough times and that the economic prospects were not good, that there would be only a 0.7 per cent increase in the gross national product, that business investments would drop by about 10 per cent in 1958 and would be likely to continue to drop in 1959, they did nothing about it either. They painted a glowing picture and all they have done is to state they are going to reconvert Canadian bonds and to increase the interest rates in order to get back to the high interest rate policy which they condemned the former government for having so long followed.
The Minister of Finance this afternoon talked about increasing unemployment figures and he took satisfaction-and this is what amazed me-in the employment figures for June, which he said were only 40,000 less than one year earlier. Just 40,000 worse than when the Liberals were in power, and the Conservatives painted such a terrible picture of conditions when the Liberals formed the government in Canada. Now that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues are in charge of the administration, however, the prospects for employment are worse, to say nothing of the existing unemployment situation. In June, instead of 162,000 persons without jobs and seeking work-as there were last June when this government took office-after the Minister of Finance has brought in his budget, after the government has read, studied, digested and concealed this report, unemployment is twice as great.
There is only one statement of the minister's which struck a somewhat sympathetic note with me, and that was when he was speaking of the rather weak amendment from the official opposition. If that amendment was a bit anaemic we hope to give it a blood transfusion, and it is my pleasure at this time to move:
That the amendment be amended by adding the words:
"and further that its action in ignoring 'The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958' as indicated

by the reported and undenied excerpts from it, has prolonged the recession and has caused suffering for thousands of Canadians because of unemployment."

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Rubbish.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: There are two things involved in this debate. One is the attitude of the government which says, "If the former government did something it is wrong, but if we do it, it is right." Secondly, the attitude of this government in having failed to act on this very important set of recommendations in order to provide full employment and a buoyant economy in 1958.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under our form of administration in Canada the anonymity and the integrity of the public service is essential for the maintenance of good government and that is the principle behind the amendment moved in this house last night by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). We have now been confronted with another amendment and I have just had an opportunity to glance quickly at its terms. My immediate reaction is that it would be difficult to fully accept its terms unless the Prime Minister is prepared to do what the Leader of the Opposition asked last night, namely to give us the opportunity of knowing precisely, in its full form, the nature of the economic survey which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated a few weeks ago would be made available only at the beginning of 1959.
We have had a defence of this attitude from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I would have thought, however, that in accordance w:th the position he holds, both as leader of the house and as the Queen's first minister, the Prime Minister would have regarded it as his duty to make a statement on Saturday last, or certainly not later than Monday, with regard to what is alleged to be the disclosure of a document which, in accordance with his own language and view as stated in this house a few weeks ago, is of a confidential character and is one which would not be made available to parliament until the beginning of 1959.
Instead we have had inadequate replies to our interrogations by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), and the defence of the government has been made by the Minister of Finance. But not a word has been said regarding the charge implied in the speeches which have been made on this side of the house or as to the terms implicit in the amendment moved by the Leader of
Canadian Economic Outlook the Opposition. It was, rather, for the Minister of Finance who, notwithstanding the fact that he delivered the longest budget speech in Canadian history-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh no.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -to think it was of such value that within two months it ought to be repeated again, in the same chamber where originally delivered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You invited it- you and your leader.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The question before us is this: are we to regard as legitimate the practice that our public servants and cabinet ministers should have the right to disclose to parliament or to other agencies, or to the nation at large, documents prepared for the confidential use of members of the government? How are we going to be able to carry on government in a country such as ours, and on lines such as are the practices and traditions in the United Kingdom, if public servants, selected on the basis of merit, for their training, and their competence, are going to have their anonymity destroyed; if they are going to be placed in the position of knowing that on some occasion the administration, or a member of the administration, may disclose to the public information given confidentially to a minister or to the government as a whole? That is the serious issue involved in this particular amendment, and it does not warrant the adjectives or the characterization given to it by the Minister of Finance who has acted, during the past two hours, in a most irresponsible manner. He is the recipient, as is the Prime Minister, of confidential documents from time to time which have to do with the conduct of government both on the domestic and international level. What the Leader of the Opposition has done has been to bring home to the government and to the house the importance of maintaining the principle of public service integrity and anonymity.
But this principle has been violated in this instance by an alert and ingenious newspaperman who was able, apparently, to provide for his newspaper certain excerpts from a document which has been denied this house. In asking that this document be tabled, the only reason why we are doing so is because of the fact that publication has taken place outside this house, and the only way to clear up this matter is, as the Globe and Mail said this morning, for the government to table the whole document so that this practice will not be repeated. I say now to the Prime Minister that if he wishes to live up to the implications of his reply the other day he should take the

Canadian Economic Outlook course suggested by the Globe and Mail, a newspaper which, generally, is not unfriendly to him and to his government.
But this whole business did not begin within recent days. It began on January 20 last. That is the situation, and I know it is one that greatly disturbs the Prime Minister at this very moment. That is why he did not rise and speak at the beginning of this debate; that is why he did not, as Prime Minister, rise on a question of privilege on Saturday last and take a course which a prime minister under our constitutional tradition and practice should have taken, and which has been taken by his predecessors on other occasions.
He was precluded from taking that course by two inconsistent positions; first, that taken in answering a question put to him a few weeks ago, when he was asked to table the report by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), and then by his own action on January last. His action and his utterances on January 20 last are now well known to this house and to the country. The previous administration, he argued, was responsible for unemployment. This government, of which he, the right hon. gentleman, is Prime Minister, was saddled with a legacy left to it by the previous administration. "Why do I say that?" said the Prime Minister. "I say so because I have here a document which records the fact that the former administration knew that the economic situation which now confronts the nation would eventuate." This was a document which the Prime Minister admitted, after persistent questioning by the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, was marked "confidential". Of course, he would table the document readily, having been requested to do so by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Did not the hon. gentleman say he must table it?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Quite correct-that the hon. gentleman must table it, having already read it. Under rule 217, the Prime Minister had no other recourse. But he should not have waited for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to suggest that the document be tabled. What did the Prime Minister do? He read excerpts from this confidential document and did the very thing which the Minister of Trade and Commerce now says the reporter of the Toronto Star should not have done.
Here is what the right hon. gentleman said at page 3522 of Hansard for January 20, 1958;
I intend to establish as clearly as the printed word will make possible that during the months

of March, April, May until June 10, my hon. friends concealed from the Canadian people the facts. They know that.
I well remember the force and the fervour which accompanied the use of those words by the Prime Minister. And then, even stronger, at page 3526 of Hansard for the same date he said:
Today one looks back and realizes that these men who were in power did not do that of which my hon. friend spoke in such colourful terms the other night. He said we must not conceal facts, but I put it to the hon. members opposite-every one of them in the official opposition-that they hid the facts; they concealed the record; they did not let the Canadian people know what was taking place.
The Prime Minister argued that this economic survey of 1957, marked "confidential", prepared for the private use of members of the government by officials in the Department of Trade and Commerce, should have been made known, should have been tabled, should have been revealed to the Canadian people before the 21st of June, 1957. That is what the Prime Minister was arguing. He attacked the new leader of the Liberal party that night with vehemence, and used a method that I do not think has very often been employed in this house, particularly by one who holds the high office of Prime Minister. He said, in effect: what does it matter if this is a document which was prepared by the public service for the confidential advice of a minister of the crown? It will suit my political purpose. I will vanquish the Leader of the Opposition if I simply reveal this document in a dramatic way on the occasion of his first speech as leader of the Liberal party. I will satisfy my followers; I will gain votes in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
That is what
he did.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: The minister says "that is what he did", and he is right. And I would think, in view of the attitude taken by the Prime Minister with regard to the 1958 survey, that that is not a very proud achievement for the hon. member to recall on this occasion.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You fellows hid that report for 20 years.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
If it was right for the previous administration to take the people of Canada into their confidence with regard to the report of 1957-and I say the government was justified in not revealing a document that had been prepared by the public service under the circumstances I have mentioned-if it was right and if it was the duty of the government to lay this information

before the Canadian people and before parliament, I ask the Prime Minister now, urging him to take part in this debate, to tell the house, having in mind the record in this matter, having in mind the way in which he used the 1957 report on January 20 last, and having in mind what he told the Canadian people about the way the previous administration had kept and withheld secrets from the Canadian people, how in the parliament of our country he can possibly justify refusing at this time to do what the Leader of the Opposition has requested, to do what the Toronto Globe and Mail urged this morning should be done, and table that document so we can find out whether or not the partial publication of this in the Toronto Star was taken from the economic survey of 1958.
No amount of debate, no amount of histrionics, no amount of subterfuge or irrelevancy in debate by the Prime Minister who is a past master at it will be able to provide a justification for not answering the question which I now put. Why will he not in the month of August 1958 in connection with a report prepared for this year table that report when he urged that a similar report prepared for 1957 by the same people and under the same auspices and for the same purposes be tabled?
The Prime Minister receives young visitors in his office frequently and tells them about the history of parliament, and about our free institutions and I really think he is to be commended for that because the people of Canada must look to their prime ministers for exemplary conduct. But I ask him in this instance as man to man, does he not realize that having taken the position he did the only way in which he can live up to the high standards he has set for himself and so properly is to take the same course as Prime Minister in 1958 that he took in the month of January prior to the general elections which resulted in his return to office? That surely is a request based upon an unanswerable argument. There can be no question about it. The only reason the Prime Minister can have for not revealing this information is that it bears out exactly what the Leader of the Opposition said last night and which some of us said during the course of the debate, and that is that the budget prepared by the Minister of Finance was not in harmony at least with the economic report prepared for 1958 by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The Minister of Finance says he has other sources on which he must rely, the Bank of Canada and his own official advisors of the Department of Finance. That is true, of course, but now that this document has been partially revealed and in my judgment only
Canadian Economic Outlook for that reason we are entitled to have the full report so we can ascertain whether or not the conclusions of the Minister of Finance with regard to the future are in harmony, at any rate with this one particular report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You did not accept those conclusions anyway.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that I do not accept those conclusions but that is not the question. The only question before us is whether or not this government, having refused to table a document which it said we should have tabled in 1957, is prepared to exercise its responsibilities in accordance with our law as provided in the Official Secrets Act. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) will, I hope, give careful consideration to what I am now going to argue.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce denied yesterday that he had said to any newspaperman that he was "running this thing down" to use his own words as contained in his statement of privilege yesterday. I have before me the Ottawa Journal of today in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is reported as having told Mr. James McCook of that newspaper, one of the most reliable men in the press gallery-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I am glad that hon. gentlemen opposite applaud newspaper people because this government yesterday and on other occasions, as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has reminded us, has not always acknowledged the objective treatment given by members of the press gallery with regard to its policies and statements. Here is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce is reported by Mr. McCook to have said yesterday after this debate:
Mr. Churchill told the Journal outside the house that he had taken only these steps when informed of the article published in Toronto:
1.	Asked for the number of copies of the confidential report issued and the distribution list.
2.	Asked for the names of those who prepared the report.
And then the article goes on in these words:
The minister said that the next step, if any, by the government or himself had not been decided.
Does the government not regard the publication of even a partial report as a development that is of the utmost concern to it as a government particularly in the light of the fact that the Prime Minister said, notwithstanding what he had said in the month of January, that this economic survey for 1958 could not be made public now in the interests of the nation, to paraphrase his words, until some time at the beginning of 1959? Is there

Canadian Economic Outlook no responsibility on the part of the government to pursue this matter? Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce done nothing more than to ask for the names of those who prepared the report and asked about the number of copies of the confidential report that were issued? Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce now deny that this report goes to every minister of the crown? Did he have to inquire who prepared this report? This report goes to him first and presumably after he has perused it it goes to the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and other members of the government.
Is this the extent of the investigation being made by this government with regard to a document which the Prime Minister said in the interests of the nation could not be given to the parliament of Canada and to the people until the beginning of 1959? Is that the extent of the investigation? Is this matter of no concern to the Minister of Justice? Has it not concerned the Prime Minister? I would call the attention both of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice to section 4 subsection 4 of the Official Secrets Act to be found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, volume III, chapter 198 which reads as follows:
4. (4) Every person who
(a)	retains for any purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state any official document, whether or not completed or issued for use, when he has no right to retain it, or when it is contrary to his duty to retain it, or fails to comply with any directions issued by any government department or any person authorized by such department with regard to the return or disposal thereof; or
(b)	allows any other person to have possession of any official document issued for his use alone, or communicates any secret official code word or pass word so issued, or, without lawful authority or excuse, has in his possession any official document or secret official code word or pass word issued for the use of some person other than himself, or on obtaining possession of any official document by finding or otherwise, neglects or fails to restore it to the person or authority by whom or for whose use it was issued, or to a police constable; is guilty of an offence under this act.
That is a very important statute. If one looks at the most recent discussion in the house based on that act he will find that in introducing amendments to the act the government of the day postulated as one of the reasons for the legislation that the public service could carry on under our system of government in a way that would preserve its integrity and not invade the anonymity which public servants under our system have a right to expect. It is the duty of the government not to make the halfhearted investigation indicated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, after the fourth day, now says, "I will find out how many copies there are, I will find out the name of the men who

wrote the report", notwithstanding that the two authors, if the papers are correct, are well known officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce of which the minister apparently is not so fully cognizant at least in so far as this particular is concerned.
Is the matter to stop there? Has the Prime Minister asked his colleagues how this document left the secret compartment that it was supposed to have until the beginning of 1959, according to his revised version of how a government should treat this confidential and secret document prepared for the use of the administration by the public service, this post-election version as the Leader of the Opposition mentions. Has any inquiry been made of his colleagues? Was it given out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith)? I do not believe it was. Was it given out by the Minister of Justice? Was it given out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself? It would be hard to believe that it was given out by the Minister of Finance because he said he had not seen it. Apparently he prepared his budget without referring to it, without knowing anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: What are you talking about?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I am asking the Minister of Finance, did he give it out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: No, you made a statement and not a very reliable one, either.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I am sure the Prime Minister did not. Did the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) inadvertently give it out?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: He does not give anything out.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Other ministers are not here. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) is not here. His seatmate is not here. I cannot ask them. The Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) looks at me so genially that I wonder whether he could have possibly given it out. I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) would not. I think he would be too prudent to allow himself to do that. At any rate he was engaged in the interests of the nation at a conference outside this country at the time, I presume.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: In January?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: No, this document was given out only within the last few days.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: How do you know?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Because it only appeared in the Toronto Star on Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You have some information.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I like to see the
Prime Minister jump at that last remark. I know him so well and I simply want to anticipate the Prime Minister. I simply want to say to the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Did you have it? Come clean.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -that I forewarn him that I knew nothing about the document and if I did-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Come, come!

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
-the Prime
Minister would have been the first to know about it, as he knows.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: What about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) and my genial friend who sits next to him looking at me so affectionately at this moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Don't kid yourself.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You are doing us a lot of good, Paul.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: In view of the importance of our mineral wealth, did he decide to give it out? Perhaps he does not know the newspaper or the reporter in question. But there are at least 18 or 20 members of the government, every one of whom has a copy of the document, and they may well rise in their places and tell us whether they can say "Mea culpa, mea culpa" or "Mea maxima culpa."

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is what you say.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The reason I say they could easily have given out this postelection version is that they gave out the earlier one. The Prime Minister himself gave it out when on January 20, 1958, he said, "I have no hesitation; here is the confidential document that reveals the state of the nation and which is responsible for the situation that now confronts us." On the basis of that kind of reasoning, why should the Prime Minister not have given out this particular version? I am not suggesting that he did but why should he not have? He had no hesitation in doing so in the month of January in a debate in the house.
The Minister of Finance seeks to escape the terms of the amendment before us by drawing a red herring and telling us again about the classical words and the great thoughts involved in his monumental budget. I say to the Minister of Finance: What we are anxious to find out and what the people of Canada are anxious to find out is whether or not the Minister of Finance, in the framing of that budget, took into account this 57071-3-197
Canadian Economic Outlook particular report because according to the report there are some very serious variations between the position taken by the Minister of Finance and the position taken in the report as it appeared in the Toronto Star.
Here is what the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, as found on page 1235 of Hansard:
-with due regard for the resourcefulness of the Canadian people and the determination of this government I have no hesitation in budgeting on the basis of a resumption of the rise in incomes and production.
The Toronto Star version of the economic survey for 1958 reads as follows in this particular, to quote from Mr. Harrison's article:
There is little basis for anticipating the renewal of any significant upward trend in over-all production and employment before the latter part of the year at least. In view of the downward momentum now present in the economy it is questionable whether any firming trend in the latter part of the year would be sufficient to bring overall production for 1958 as a whole up to the level of the preceding year.
I do not know whether or not that was contained in the report but what I do know and what the Minister of Finance knows, notwithstanding his diversionary tactics today and last night, is that that is alleged to be taken from the economic survey for 1958 which presumably was considered by the Minister of Finance in the formulation of his budget. If that is the case, then the Minister of Finance did not tell the Canadian people what some of his advisers had urged him to consider in the formulation of his policy. He tried today to substantiate his prognostications for the future. He referred to the increase in export trade and he referred to certain other indices. What he did not do was to tell the house that unemployment today in this month of August, a period of traditional recovery, is double what it was this time a year ago. The Minister of Finance did not indicate today or in his budget-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You are just guessing again.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -nor did he give any reasons this afternoon-my hon. friend says I am guessing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You have done a lot of guessing.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: There can be no doubt that the Minister of Finance has disregarded the advice of his constitutional advisers, of his financial advisers-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Such nonsense!

Canadian Economic Outlook

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -and has painted an economic picture that is not in harmony-even with the facts as they are now known.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is nonsense.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), has he consulted certain other government departments? Has he asked them what they consider will be the level of unemployment in the month of September? What it will be in the month of October? I have made certain projections that are now appearing in the Monetary Times, indicating that in the month of December we will possibly have as many as one million men and women who will be unplaced applicants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I hope they realize how unreliable you are as a prognosticator.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I ask the minister to remember these words when, at the end of six months' time, we confront one another in this house and are able to see whether or not his optimistic view was in harmony with the prognostications he gave in his budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You were a great exaggerator last January.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I well remember the statement my hon. friend made when we asked him to reduce the excise tax on automobiles last fall. He said there was no serious unemployment in the automobile industry. Today he gets up in this house and talks about the economic picture of our country as though there were no unemployed people. In my own city of Windsor today, in the month of August, there are almost 12,000 men and women out of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? He has made a statement that the number of men out of work at this moment in Windsor is 12,000. I wonder what action he and his government took when the unemployed in the city of Windsor numbered 11,220 in July, 1954 and 10,432 in 1956?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is a very fair question. What did the government of which I was a member do? This government courageously pursued a policy-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -that put men and women to work in this country, with the result that during the time when Mr. St. Laurent was prime minister we had the highest level of prosperity in Canadian history.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You never once opened your mouth to advocate a decrease in the excise tax on automobiles.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
My friends say we are conveyers of doom, and I want to pursue that statement. I would remind my hon. friends of what the former leader of their party, Hon. Mr. Drew, said on March 29, 1955, as recorded at page 2498 of Hansard:
I regret that anyone would suggest that a discussion on unemployment is an attempt to undermine confidence, If there is any attempt to undermine confidence on that basis, then of course it must come from the agency of the government which gives the figures. The figures that have been used are given by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Then he went on to say it was his duty in opposition to point out the situation as he saw it to the government. Now, that is why we have done the same thing. I say again, as I said during the budget debate, that the Minister of Finance should indicate unequivocally whether or not this report was used; whether or not he has lived up to the advice given him on all fronts by those in the public service whose duty it is to advise the Minister of Finance and the government as a whole.
Why should the government take this pious attitude which the Minister of Finance has taken when noting that in the Toronto Star it is alleged that there are certain excerpts from a genuine government document? Why should the Minister of Finance, in fairness to the country and to the responsibilities of his office, not say, yes, unfortunately this document has been revealed in part. Now that it has been revealed, there is only one course open and that is to place it on the table so that we can settle this matter once and for all. That would be a courageous attitude for the Minister of Finance to take. Then we would know where we are at. Then, having done that, the Minister of Finance could also take this position: Let us now decide never again to do what was done on January 20 last by the Prime Minister of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You did not like it, did you?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I certainly did not like it, and I am surprised the Minister of Public Works, a member of the government of Canada, should say that he liked his Prime Minister revealing, for the purpose of an election advantage, a document that was marked "Private and Confidential". The Prime Minister has said, "Oh, no, I cannot give this document for 1958; I have the heavy responsibility of government, and I must discharge my responsibility in the light of our traditional practice. I cannot tell parliament, I cannot tell the nation what my advisers tell us about the economic conditions-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Certainly not.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Someone says "Certainly not", and yet in the month of January last the Prime Minister did that very thing. Last night mention was made of the Prime Minister's speech at Edmonton, as reported in the Ottawa Journal. The Leader of the Opposition was challenged to refer to this. I now have the clipping and here is what the Prime Minister said in Edmonton when he was confronting the public and complaining about how we had withheld important information from the Canadian people. I can see the hon. gentleman speaking to 5,000 people in Edmonton, and telling them exactly the opposite to what he told us only a few days ago when he said he could not reveal this document. The article states:
"They concealed", he said of the Liberal cabinet ministers.
"They covered up. They hid. They knew but they did not act. They were warned that a serious situation was developing in this country . . . in effect the beginning of a recession".
All of the Liberal cabinet ministers had received the report, he said.
"None of them read it. All of them hid it."
Those are the words of this great saviour of human liberty-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -who went the length and breadth of this country revealing the contents of a document which he says now he cannot give to this house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is the same speech you made during the election campaign.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: My friend says that is the same speech I made during the election, and my friend is right. The only difference between my speech during the election and the speeches which were made by the Prime Minister is that his-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Were successful.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -because they were so attractive in deception, were able to capture support which will never again come to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Will my friend permit a question? When he talks about deception, will he tell the house why it was, in his billboards and publicity during the election campaign, he did not use the word "Liberal"?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I have a very good answer. First of all, I am well known as a Liberal. Secondly, I was in Prince Albert once during the election campaign and I saw the committee rooms of the present Prime Minister. There was not one reference to the 57071-3-1974
Canadian Economic Outlook word "Conservative", or "Progressive Conservative"; it was called the "John Diefenbaker Committee".

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: What was your majority?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Using the foregoing as my arguments, I urge the house to accept this amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: After listening to the attempts of my hon. friends opposite in both the official opposition and the C.C.F. to work this house up into a state of righteous indignation over what they allege are the misdemeanours of this government, and after observing how lamentably short they fell even of the objective which they have set themselves, one can understand why it is they are driven back to the subterfuge of attempting to induce the government to do the very thing which they themselves say should not be done.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: For the reasons given.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: One can understand also the skill which hon. gentlemen opposite have achieved in this sort of game when one remembers the numerous holidays they used to take when they were in power on the occasions when they went fishing. What we have seen here is the most gigantic fishing expedition that it has ever been the pleasure or the misfortune of the House of Commons to see in my history.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: The minister is still very young.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: What we have seen is from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) down an attempt to inveigle this government into a position where it would have no recourse but to do the very thing which hon. gentlemen say should not be done, namely to table a document which they themselves say is confidential and should not be tabled.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Because part of it you have already given out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: It certainly is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
If one were to take my hon. friends opposite seriously-but they themselves have precluded us from doing that by their own remarks-one would simply have to read back to them the remarks they themselves have made in this debate in order to dispose of the motion and the amendment they have used. This righteous indignation, this attempt of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and especially of the Leader of the Opposition last night to suggest that this

Canadian Economic Outlook document should be tabled is seen for the narrowest, meanest and poorest disguise in which any opposition ever attempted to close a motion. Let me read to my hon. friends some of their remarks. On no fewer than three occasions the Leader of the Opposition said this sort of document should not be tabled. Last night he said this:
I think it is regrettable-
He was referring to the possibility of tabling the document; what document they refer to, I do not yet know.
-that this should have to be done in the interests of clarifying this situation. In the past these reports have been considered as confidential, secret documents from expert civil servants to their ministers. For many years, they were treated as such. In the past, the previous government had not made these reports public, and for very good reasons.
That is the Leader of the Opposition speaking, as reported at page 3072 of Hansard.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Would the minister tell us what his own attitude is to the tabling of these documents?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: If the hon. member would identify the documents.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I shall be delighted to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I did not know there was more than one document under discussion at the present time.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: All right. I should like to ask the Minister of Justice-and I say again "these documents"-what his attitude is to the tabling of the Canadian Economic Outlook for 1957 and the Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958. Does he think there is one rule for one and another rule for the other? I should like to have a plain answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. The hon. gentleman has asked a plain question, Mr. Speaker. You might almost call it a simple question. It is a simple question because the answer has been given over and over again. The economic report of 1957 was tabled in January of 1958.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: And your leader said it should have been tabled in June of 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: My leader said no such thing.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: He said it over and over again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not content with asking innumerable silly questions which

get him into more trouble than if he remained silent but he even interrupts while he is sitting down. My hon. friend obviously cannot understand the meaning of plain English. If he will go back and read the speech of the Prime Minister on January 20 of this year he will find that what the Prime Minister accused my hon. friends opposite of was of having concealed the facts. At no time did the Prime Minister say that the government should have tabled the document.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Did he not?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: On only one occasion did the Prime Minister say that the government had concealed the document. At no time did he say that they should table it. He said the government had hidden the facts. He said that the government had misled the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: There are seven pages there, starting at page 3523.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: If my hon. friends will permit me to make my own speech I should be obliged to them. Theirs were rather poor. I beg them not to spoil mine.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That would be impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
My hon. friends will find that the Prime Minister as recorded at page 3525 of Hansard of January 20 of this year said this:
They did not realize the situation or if they did so they concealed the facts from the Canadian people;-
And at page 3526:
-they hid the facts; they concealed the record; they did not let the Canadian people know what was taking place.
Then at page 3527:
But they did nothing during the session to bring about changes in legislation to meet the situation of which they had been warned.
Then again:
They kept it from the Canadian people.
Here is the only one I have been able to find with reference to concealing the document:
-and now, for political purposes, having concealed this document, they have the effrontery to pretend to the Canadian people that we are responsible.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman read a few words before that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
At page 3528 we find this:
Why did hon. members opposite, in the idealistic vein of the hon. Leader of the Opposition, not reveal these facts? Why did they not act on them, even if they did not think fit to reveal them?
Then at page 3530:
You concealed the facts.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Let me conclude this part of my remarks. I would ask my hon. friend to allow me to do that.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: All right.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The whole tenor of the Prime Minister's remarks was that the hon. gentlemen then in power concealed the facts from the Canadian people; that having been warned of the economic situation and of the dangers in the economic climate which then were known to their expert advisers and which became evident in their results about June
1957	and July 1957,-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Which the Prime Minister denied in November.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: -in spite of these danger signs, hon. gentlemen opposite concealed them and introduced a budget which flew in the very face of the warnings they had received from their economic advisers. That was the sense of the Prime Minister's charge.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Will the hon. member read to the house the exchange between the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the Prime Minister as found at page 3530 and following in Hansard?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I have read it. I do not think it is necessary to read it again in detail.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I have said that I do not think it is necessary to read it in detail again. The then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked whether the document had been tabled and the Prime Minister said:
If it has not been tabled my hon. friend has added one more example to the record of concealment by my hon. friends opposite.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: And we could not table it after June 21.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Go on to page 3531.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
We find this:
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it was hidden away so well we just found it.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Of course that statement was not correct.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
From what I have read, Mr. Speaker, it becomes obvious that the tenor of the Prime Minister's charge in January of
1958	was that my hon. friends had concealed the facts from the Canadian people and in their budget had taken a course which was revealed to be a course of folly and of recklessness in the light of the facts that they had, in the light of facts of which they had
Canadian Economic Outlook been warned as far back as January of last year. The very great difference between the situation then and the situation now is that the economic report of which my hon. friends allege extracts have appeared in the Toronto Star is a current document and for the reasons which the Prime Minister gave last January or earlier in this session should not be tabled at this time. My hon. friends admit that it should not be tabled. They say that these documents should not be tabled when they are current because they say that the anonymity of civil service advice should be preserved. Yet on the other hand they turn around and do their best to trap us into such steps as will then enable them to demand the tabling of the document.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
A trap of your own
construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is the type of fishing expedition in which my hon. friends have been engaged. But however attractive the bait, it has not been successful; and may I say that the bait was not very attractive; it was a little bit old; it was a little bit worn. Those of us, Mr. Speaker, who may engage in angling as distinguished from fly fishing know how sometimes when the worms have been on the hook for a while they do not look too appetizing. The efforts made by my hon. friends opposite to bait their hook remind me of this kind of old, waterlogged, worn-out wormy bait that we have seen occasionally on these fishing expeditions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: He can end this argument at once or this fishing expedition. Will he now deny the accuracy of the excerpts from these reports that have appeared in the press?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: If they are denied, you do not have to produce them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That bait is getting more tired and disgusting looking on every occasion it is used. It is the same bait with which he tried to bait his hook last night, but it did not work.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Why don't you deny it?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Because you are caught on a hook.

I would like to impress upon the hon. member that if he thinks there is anything of any nature whatsoever, from what he has heard, which he thinks is inaccurate or unjust, then he could bring it

before the committee on privileges and elections. Without answering what was said or attempting to give evidence as to what was said, the hon. gentleman has a right at his hand, and I read from citation 105 of Beauchesne's fourth edition at page 96:
It is the practice in the House of Commons to bring up a question of privilege after prayers, and before the house has taken up the orders of the day. Only in very aggravated cases, requiring the immediate interposition of the house, will any business be suddenly interrupted. May says, that the proceedings of the house may be interrupted at any moment, save during the process of a division, by a motion based on a matter of privilege, when a matter has recently arisen which directly concerns the privileges of the house, and in that case the house will entertain the motion forthwith. Bourinot quotes an ancient authority as saying: "Whether any question is or is not before the house, and even in the midst of another discussion, if a member should rise to complain of a breach of privileges of the house, they have always instantly heard him."
It is perfectly clear that had the hon. gentleman intended to raise as a matter of substance the matter which he raised by inference in his speech this afternoon and if, and I said this afternoon, he had the courage of the convictions on the basis of which he made those statements, it is open to him at any time to bring forward a motion of privilege and in that motion of privilege to state what it is he has in mind. The house would then, according to the citations I have read, have to take it into consideration immediately, in my submission, and I therefore suggest once again that hon. members should have the courtesy to accept the assurances of the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to his statement made yesterday. If they do not, there is only one course open to them which in decency they should take, and that is to raise the matter directly on a question of privilege so that the matter can be dealt with in the way in which it should be dealt with, and in these circumstances there is no doubt what would be the outcome. I suggest, therefore, that the hon. member for Assiniboia, apparently not being prepared to take that course, should admit that what he said about the Minister of Trade and Commerce was quite unjustified, and not that which he would like to see remain on the record.
It has become increasingly evident that this thing is a fishing expedition. All hon. members opposite want to do is to have us table a report which they themselves say should not be tabled at this stage in the House of Commons. The answer to the whole situation is that circumstances here are entirely different from the circumstances when the report was produced and tabled in January of this year. That was a report on the economic forecast for 1957. The budget had been based

on it; the budget had been brought in and passed, and, some 12 or 12 months after that report had been prepared it was tabled by the Prime Minister as part of the record; part of the record which should have been placed before the Canadian people to show the extent to which the previous government had, for political advantage, disregarded the warnings of its economic advisers and attempted to convince the Canadian people that all was rosy when, in fact, they knew it was not rosy.
In this case, any economic report made for 1958 would have been made a matter of a few months ago. The budget in all its stages has not yet been concluded and no attempt has been made, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, to do other than lay the economic facts before the Canadian people, balancing the prospects for good against indications which may not be so attractive. There has been no attempt to mislead the Canadian people as there was in March 1957-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Let us examine what the Prime Minister said. When I spoke in that debate I held in my hand the original which had been tabled in the house and it took me many hours before I was able to get it-the original which the Prime Minister had had in his hand at the time he spoke-and in that original it was clear that some pages had been torn out because the tabs had been left on. I was not able to say at that time and neither am I able to say now that it was the Prime Minister who had torn them off and I am not even suggesting he did but the statement I made then and the statement I make now is that the four pages that were marked "secret" had been torn off by someone. Of that I think there is no doubt. The remaining pages were marked "confidential".
In any event here was a report, secret and confidential, which was tabled contrary to the practice and the tradition of this house and I venture to say to the Prime Minister with all respect to the position he now occupies that I doubt very much if his predecessor in office-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Or any of them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
-or indeed any of them would have done any such thing as that which was done on the occasion of that debate.
May I return to the Minister of Finance and that very sarcastic, violent and vituperative speech of his which he made last night. The minister in his budget speech did not even indicate that he did not take into account the report concerning the Canadian outlook for 1958. Because of the attitude now taken the whole civil service is damaged. That, of course, is typical of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: How ridiculous can you be?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The minister says how
ridiculous that statement is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I asked you how ridiculous you could be and now you are going on to prove it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Last January in announcing additional grants to the provinces the Minister of Finance did not even use the advice of his civil servants in making the calculations as to what the amount should have been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: How do you know?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I presume he did not because he rose at a later date and had to change and amend the amounts which he tabled at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Another assumption. Why not get some facts once in a while?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Ask the minister if he did.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
My facts are certainly as accurate as some of the facts which the Minister of Finance put on the record last night and I hope that if he ever finds time to read his speech he will observe what inconsequential statements he made over a period of several hours.
Let me come back to what I was saying to the minister. He has shown the same attitude here with reference to this discussion. He has failed to appreciate the importance of the contributions of his advisers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Why not make a speech instead of reading it?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Look who is talking about reading.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: He displayed the same attitude which caused him not long ago to slap down the governor of the Bank of Canada. That is exactly what he did. He tried to play the same record which the Prime Minister played last January and I can assure the house that that record fell pretty flat last night and even flatter this afternoon when the minister sat down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Even flatter now, eh?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
That indicates to me that what has happened was that the members of the government were not prepared for this amendment. They expected an amendment which was other than this and I believe I can say with some degree of accuracy that what was expected on the other side of the house was a demand for the production of the 1958 hidden report. Hon. gentlemen opposite were ready to argue that point. And the interesting thing about it is that the Minister of Finance was caught off base. He expected something in the amendment which was not there. He was caught off base and instead of dealing with the amendment as he should have he proceeded to re-read his budget speech over and over again, a speech which was very
Canadian Economic Outlook monotonous when he read it on budget night and still more monotonous when he gave it to us again last evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I expected a manly amendment, not that puny excuse for an amendment.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I return to what I was discussing when the house took recess at six o'clock I should like to say a word concerning the subamendment of the C.C.F. party. When the hon. member for Essex East spoke earlier in the debate he indicated that at first glance he was not disposed to support the subamendment and I can say as well that when I looked at it I was not, at first glance, disposed to support it either. If the government would table the whole document we would then wish to consult the document before basing any vote upon its contents but all we have are excerpts published by the Toronto Star. They indicate that the Minister of Finance disregarded the advice of the experts and in the light of what information is available to us we feel we should vote for the subamendment.
Returning now to the discussion that took place earlier, upon the reading of Hansard, I was somewhat surprised, when I was dealing with the secret document, at the intervention made by the Prime Minister. He said of me, "This is completely unworthy of you."

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: No, no. Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and I were talking back and forth. The Leader of the Opposition made some observation and I made an observation which had no reference to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). There was a cross-fire between us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I am the guilty one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I do not know what the statement was.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I am very happy to hear the Prime Minister say that it is not I who is unworthy. In any event, I want to come back to the discussion earlier so that there

Canadian Economic Outlook can be no doubt about the nature of the report that was under discussion on January 20 because there certainly seemed to be some doubt in the Prime Minister's mind as to exactly what it was. I should like to refer to the debate which took place on January 21, 1958, page 3559 of Hansard. At that time I had made the following comment:
I have another remark to make with reference to this document, Mr. Speaker. The document I hold in my hand is marked "confidential", but something has been taken from it. I make this statement not because I was a member of the government, since I have not been a member of the government for the last three years. But look at this document. A page has been torn from it, and those who have torn the page off here left a fragment of it there and on the back of it is a blue portion indicating it has been tampered with. I am informed by my former colleagues that its covers were blue; and that part of the report which normally indicates . . . that it is a secret document. Therefore, I ask this question. Why was this tabled and marked "confidential", whereas the rest of it is secret? Where is the rest of it? Where are the other pages which should be attached to this?
I should like to quote from a statement in the same volume at page 4199 attributed to the Right Hon. Mr. Gardiner as follows:
When I got my copy on March 29, 1957, I made a note on it to send it west. I took it out west and read it. Of course, I had to get it back again and that document is marked, right on the front page, with the word "secret". Of course, I did not read it to the press and to my constituents out west at election time. And then on the second page it is marked "secret" again and, of course, I did not read that document to others.
I simply desired to put those two quotations on Hansard so that there might be no doubt about the statement I made earlier as to the fact that this document was not so much a confidential document as it was a secret document. Now, I presume from the agitation I saw the Prime Minister display earlier that he will take part in the debate and I hope that he will as I also hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will take part in the debate. After all, this document was prepared by officers of his department. They are the ones who prepared both the 1957 and 1958 documents. He has made certain statements challenging the accuracy of press reports and it would seem to me that certainly he, of all ministers, should take part in the discussion.
We were wondering, therefore, just at what stage the Prime Minister will enter the debate. This afternoon he indicated that he intended to contribute to the discussion. He threw the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) into the debate last night and then today the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). The Minister of Justice was doing so poorly before six o'clock that he was scratched before he had a chance to finish his speech.

All this, it seems to me, points to a speech by the Prime Minister in an effort to prop up the sagging prestige of the government in this debate. But knowing the Prime Minister as I do and having a great deal of respect for his ability and skill, I have a feeling that when he does enter the debate he will indicate in no uncertain terms that if he tabled this report it was at the request of members on this side of the house. I am referring, of course, to "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1957" report. I should like to say here that during the course of that debate the former member for Winnipeg North Centre challenged him to produce the document and I believe that my colleague, the hon. member for Essex East did likewise.
What I think the house should not forget, and what I think the house should have uppermost in its mind, is that the Prime Minister cannot get away from the fact that he was asked to table this document by these two hon. gentlemen, in accordance with the rules. During the period prior to six o'clock on January 20, 1958, he read at great length from the secret document. In fact, I believe he quoted some 26 excerpts from the document. He charged that it had been concealed by the former administration. He made charges that the former administration was responsible for the condition in which the country was at that time, and had concealed the evidence. After having read from that document for a period of at least two hours [DOT]-I remember the speech quite well-and quoting extracts from it at great length, under the rules of the house there was no alternative for him but to table the document.
I may wish to come back to this in a moment, but now I should like to say something about that loquacious, sarcastic, vituperative speech made by the Minister of Finance. This speech, sir, divides itself into two parts. In the first part, he poured out ridicule and scorn upon my leader without, I submit with deference, dealing with the substance of the amendment before the house. In my opinion, that speech was unworthy, if that expression can now be used by me, of the Minister of Finance. Then, too, there is another thing to which I should like to take exception, and it is that during the course of my remarks earlier today I made some reference to the Minister of Finance and from the other side of the house came the charge, "Cheap". Well, sir, there could have been nothing cheaper than that which came out of the mouth of the Minister of Finance than the reference which he made to my leader, dealing with his speech on January 20, when he stated that after that speech the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was alone and walked out

of this house without anyone accompanying him. If ever there was a cheap assertion, that was one which came from the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: It is not true because I say here, on my responsibility as a member of parliament, that I sat beside the Leader of the Opposition and I walked out of the house with him on that occasion. But I will add this, however. Last night, after the flat speech of the Minister of Finance nobody accompanied him; no one came up to his seat save the loud-mouthed Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness).

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: This business of cheap assertions is a double-edged sword and can be used by both sides of the house. It would have been a great deal better if the Minister of Finance had never used it.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hit where you can, below the belt.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hon. members opposite do not like this. I am not surprised they do not like it. They do not like any part of this debate. They are in difficulties, and about that there can be no doubt. If they are not in difficulty, why do they not table "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958"?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Parlez en frangais.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That remark from the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McPhillips) indicates the truth of my statement that members on the other side of the house are upset by this amendment; that members on the other side of the house not only do not like this amendment but find themselves considerably embarrassed. Why do they not tell us what is in the report?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You will get the business in a few minutes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: I have no doubt that in a few minutes the Prime Minister will rise and give us an example of his skill in this kind of debate. However, no matter how skilful he is he will never be able to get out of the embarrassment in which he has placed not only himself but his followers on the other side of the house.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You will come out of your trance.
