subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
If he were not embarrassed he would allow the Minister of Trade and
Canadian Economic Outlook Commerce to rise in his place and tell us what his position is. Why does not the Minister of Trade and Commerce speak?

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Because you are talking too long.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
He has no hesitation about getting up and making changes in press statements as he did earlier today and yesterday, but as yet he will not say a word. He is tongue-tied today, and that is surprising for that loquacious minister. At least, he should tell us what the position is. But no, they call on the Minister of Finance and on the Minister of Justice. Of course, without doubt, the Prime Minister will close the debate after a little while.
But I am being taken away from the subject matter of my remarks. I wanted to refer, sir, to the second part of the speech made by the Minister of Finance. The second part of his speech dealt with the economic situation in 1957, utterly disregarding the report, "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958". Really, to use his own expression, it was a runt of a speech.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: My hon. friends say "Oh", but I am using exactly the same words the Minister of Finance used. If they are applicable to the amendment, let me say that they are equally applicable to the speech made by the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: More so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
The attitude of the Minister of Finance shows that he is completely irresponsible or that he has not understood the amendment which is before the house. I should like to deal with the amendment, which can be divided into two parts. It reads as follows:
"this house is of the opinion that the actions of the government in connection with 'The Canadian Economic Outlook' have seriously weakened the value of confidential advice from civil servants with resultant damage to the proper formulation of economic and fiscal policies".
Those are the two points contained in the amendment. First, we believe that the conduct of the government has seriously weakened the benefit of confidential advice from civil servants. If this charge is justified, and the Minister of Finance did not establish that it was not, then it means that the relationship between the government and the civil service has deteriorated and has worsened. A good relationship between the two is essential in a democracy and under the rules such as we have them in this house. It is evident that the situation between the civil service and the present

Canadian Economic Outlook government has worsened and has deteriorated considerably. No one is more capable of telling us about that than the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Irresponsible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Just listen to this to see how irresponsible it is. Let me tell the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) that at least ten members of the civil service who resigned-

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Order. I am sure the hon. member who has the floor is finding difficulty with so many people interrupting. I am not sure whether he is having more difficulty from behind or in front, but from all parts of the house there seem to be constant interruptions. I would ask hon. members to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was saying that there has been a deterioration between the government and the civil service. That fact is evidenced by the resignations that have taken place, no less than a substantial number of them-I believe four or five-from the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day, dealing with that subject, said they all had good reason to resign and that they sent letters of resignation giving the reasons therefor. I am quite sure that they had good reasons to resign. I believe the minister as well as I believe the reasons given by those members of the civil service for their resignations. The point I am making is this. I am convinced in my own mind and in my own heart that these men would still be in the civil service if the former administration were still in office.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Then we have had attacks made upon the civil service by members of parliament before this report leaked out as well as since that time. These charges have been renewed without any evidence yet to justify the charge. I need only refer to the editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail and which dealt with the alternatives which could have happened in this leak. May I quote from the editorial under the name of Mr. Robert Duffy which appeared in the Globe and Mail of August 4, 1958:
That may be generally true, but in this case Trade and Commerce Minister Churchill was 

already on record with an admission made outside the house, that the newspaper extracts from the report were perfectly accurate.
In fairness to the minister, I must say that statement was denied by him earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Thank you.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
I continue:
If the ministers were merely confused, however, there was a more interesting reaction from some Conservative backbenchers. The quick suspicion was that some official had passed the secret report to the Liberals, who passed it on to the newspaper, in order to create an issue embarrassing to the government.
It may have happened that way, but there is another possibility. Conceivably, some government supporter may have disclosed the document, in pursuit of his own ends. There are rivalries within a government as well as between political parties. And as a general rule most government departments feel that the Finance Minister and the Treasury Board are not giving them enough money to spend.
That gives some indication of where the leak might have come. Then there is the attitude of the no less arrogant Minister of Agriculture who fires a member of the public service and makes criminal accusations against him which are absolutely without foundation. There is a well-known rule of law that a man is presumed innocent until found guilty. The minister reversed the rule, however, and found him guilty without trial.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Order. I would remind the hon. member that that matter was discussed at considerable length in a previous debate and is not relevant tonight.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: And his time is up.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: You hope.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as always I accept your ruling and I bow to it.
If I may, I should like to return to the arrogant Minister of Finance who has now come into the house. In his absence I was telling him that the amendment which he ignored completely dealt with a number of things, the things in particular that should have been drawn to his attention. I had arrived at the second point made in our amendment which is derived from the first and which is to the effect that the value of confidential advice from the civil service having been seriously weakened, great damage has been done to the formulation of economic and fiscal policies. We all know that in the preparation of the budget and in determining what are going to be the levels of public expenditures and taxes for a given year the government cannot escape the responsibility of making some kind of assessment of what the over-all economic outlook

and the over-all economic situation is going to be for that year. The Canadian people have the right to expect that procedure. The Canadian people have been accustomed to that procedure. The government must in fulfilling its responsibilities take the advice of its senior civil servants, get the best possible advice it can in the preparation of the budget; it should have not only the best expert advice but the best system, the best method of assessment of the economic situation, otherwise, if that were not the case, serious mistakes could be made when the estimates of public expenditure and taxes are prepared, with the result that Canadians would not benefit from the most effective policies designed to cope with any possible undesirable economic situation.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance in dealing with his budget quoted from a white paper prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce entitled "Private and Public Investment for Canada; Outlook for 1958". What he did, was to refer to that document in dealing with the composition of the gross national product, which is made up by government expenditures, exports minus imports, investments and consumer expenditures. Those added up equal the gross national product. He used the figures which are to be found at page 7 of this "Outlook for 1958". As can be found at page 1235 of Hansard, he said this:
The expanded role of social capital is illustrated in the 1958 Outlook for Private and Public Investment published by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Present investment intentions of business for capital outlays in 1958 are about 11 per cent below the 1957 level. Planned outlays for housing, government departments and institutional services on the other hand are 14 per cent higher.

There is no disagreement with respect to the fact that our civil service makes a contribution worthy of the finest traditions of public service, but he went out of his way to say that because of the fact that a number of civil servants in high positions had resigned this must have

Let me say to my hon. friend the hon. member for Laurier that some resigned from the civil service to get a better job in government than they would have had outside of it and in that respect I am sure he will require no identification; some resigned from the civil service or the public service in the expectation of greater rewards in government.
So there they sit, three of them who have at one time or another resigned from the civil or public service of Canada and have found their way into parliament. I do not think there is any argument that it is to the credit of civil servants who find they can improve their positions-and they certainly can, especially those in the higher areas of the civil service and indeed all areas of the civil service have before them at all times the magnetic attraction of far greater advantages, monetary and otherwise, than the civil service can offer-that they stay in the civil service and give to our country the benefit of their wisdom and advice.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE

I witnessed the crocodile tears of the hon. gentlemen opposite-oh, how they love the civil service, but they waited until this government came to power for the increases which we eventually brought in for former civil servants.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext: That is a noble argument.

subsubtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT ON CONFIDENTIAL ADVICE
speechtext:

member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) would acquire an even greater reputation for wisdom if he could for once maintain silence.

subsubtopic: CONVERSION LOAN, EFFECTS OF HIGHER INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance which I feel I must raise at this time because it deals with a matter which is not subject to a decision of the house in the normal course of events in that the government has undertaken an action for which, according to the authority vested in it, it did not have to ask the permission of this house. The action was taken within recent weeks as a decision of the government. I am, of course, referring to the bond conversion deal of the Conservative government, which is part of the new vision in the field of Canadian finance.
I want to be fair before I make my complaint by listing the only two advantages which I can see in this bond conversion deal so far as the people of Canada are concerned. In the first place, it is anti-inflationary in that it makes out of short term securities long term holdings and thereby removes from the potential buying power of the Canadian economy as much money as is being converted. The other advantage is that it clears the decks of the money markets of an overloading of short term securities, an overloading which was flooding the money markets.
Conversion Loan-Interest Rates
I believe, and I say this sincerely, that on the whole this government has not yet made many serious mistakes. Its sins have been mostly sins of omission. In my opinion, however, this is the first major blunder, the first major sin committed by the regime of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). The move is unprecedented in that it involves the conversion of from 40 to 60 per cent of the national public debt, depending upon the figure you take as being the real national public debt. It involves an unprecedented $6,400 million. It involves a rise in interest rates on government bonds from the 3 per cent which is now being paid to a high of 41 per cent on the converted bonds. The Tory party is here really revealing itself as the traditional high interest party which it has always been in the entire history of Canada.
It is unique in that it converts callable bonds into non-callable bonds. It is unique in that every effort is being made to see that as far as possible all conversions should be into 25-year bonds. The conversion is also unique in that it is a conversion of bonds which are as yet unmatured into bonds carrying a higher interest rate. Many governments of Canada have in past years converted or called in unmatured bonds; they have called them in for the purpose of converting them to bonds carrying a lower interest rate. However, this government, for some reason that it has not yet explained to the country, is calling in bonds, in some instances many years before the date of maturity, and offering a higher interest rate if the holders will accept the new long-term bonds.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) also announced a uniquely high rate on a short term loan when he announced that the government had arranged for $400 million until the fall at 2J per cent. That also is new as far as interest rates go for this type of money. I have read the budget speech of the Minister of Finance and I am going to say that on June 17 he did not contemplate the move he had undertaken since June 17, because throughout the budget speech the implication was very clear that the most the minister was expecting to have to convert and borrow on the money market this year was $3,400 million. I can come to only one conclusion: This deal is so unheard of and so unreasonable that the minister found, after announcing his plans in the budget, that he was unable to get the $3,400 million that he expected to raise this year; $1,900 million to meet the victory bonds that were maturing, some $700 million to carry the deficit and another $800 million, roughly, to cover what are commonly called contingent liabilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONVERSION LOAN, EFFECTS OF HIGHER INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Utterly ridiculous.

subsubtopic: CONVERSION LOAN, EFFECTS OF HIGHER INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
The government only had to convert $1,900 million worth of bonds, because that is the total that were falling due this year, and I fail to understand why the government could not wait until next year before converting the issues falling due next year, and so on. Why did they have to convert $6,400 million worth of bonds? I must ask this question: who is the boss of Canada? Is it the government which the people elected on March 31, or is it the boys on Bay street and St. James street? I ask, furthermore, if this is the pay off for the election funds of the Conservative party-a 50 per cent increase in the pay of the money lenders of Canada. I wonder what the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) would say if the school teachers, the civil servants or the farmers, or any other class of people in Canada, were to ask for a 50 per cent increase in their take home pay? Yet this is exactly what the Minister of Finance has told the money-lenders of Canada they can receive.
Not only is a bonus being paid to these people, but the government has been lavish in the commission rates which it is paying to the money-lenders for the conversion of these bonds. In addition, I notice the government has embarked on a very extensive and national publicity campaign and has inserted full page ads in every little weekly from one end of Canada to the other. The cost of the publicity of this new approach in the financing of the public debt is bound to be enormous. What the whole thing will cost, only the years can tell. I have made a very rough estimate, and I believe that over the 25-year period, assuming that the whole of this issue will be converted, and assuming that the rise in interest rates on other borrowings in Canada is going to amount to approximately three times that of the increase on the bonds, we get a gross cost to the Canadian people of $10,000 million over the next 25-year period.
This deal is already affecting other interest rates in Canada. There are many lending institutions attached to the federal government whose interest rates are directly allied to whatever interest rates the federal government agrees to pay on its long term bonds. I refer to money that is being borrowed by the people of Canada under the Central Mortgage and Housing Act, or National Housing Act loans; I refer to money being lent to the


farmers of Canada by the Canadian farm loan board, and so on. There are many other institutions in Canada through whose assistance people borrow money from government agencies, and whose interest rates are going to be very directly affected. Interest rates on provincial government obligations are bound to rise; interest rates of municipal governments, hospital boards, and school boards are also going to rise, and if these rates do not rise, these institutions will have to pay through the nose in the other way by having to sell debentures at less than par.
It is going to affect the rates at which Canadian commercial undertakings will be able to borrow money and, in addition, affect the rates which the ordinary individual will have to pay on his private borrowings. After all, why should any lending institution be very interested in lending money to an individual at 5 per cent, 5J per cent or 6 per cent if it can lend to the federal government on a 25-year non-callable basis and be assured of a return of 4J per cent? The total price that the people are going to be asked to pay for the privilege of having a Conservative government will be fantastic; the whole scheme is bound to work hardship on the ordinary taxpayers and consumers of Canada.
Why do I feel so keenly about this? Let us look at what is happening to one individual- and I am going to take as an example someone I know-someone who in wartime scraped and denied himself of many things he would liked to have had. However, he knew he was supposed to help the government to ward off inflation; he was urged to buy victory bonds to help win the war and, like the good old soul he was, he invested $2,000 of his hard-earned savings in victory bonds. After the war he found that rents had climbed sky high, and felt obliged to buy a new home. So he decided to sell his victory bonds. He took them to the bank, and what did he get? Did he get 100 cents on the dollar as the banks and insurance houses are now getting? This particular man got 93 cents, and lost $140 of his investment right there. Those who bought those bonds at a discount are now the holders of the bonds. It is estimated that only one out of ten or possibly one out of 12 of these victory bonds are now held by individuals in Canada as individuals.

speechtext: I notice, Mr. Speaker, that every time I hit the minister where it hurts the minister immediately replies by charging that everything I say is nonsense. I have grown used to that over the years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What the hon. member is saying is worse than nonsense. It is extremely harmful and mischievous.

subsubtopic: CONVERSION LOAN, EFFECTS OF HIGHER INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I know that millions of Canadians were forced by the exigencies of the situation to cash in their victory bonds and were required to accept 92 and 93 cents on the dollar. It was an inflated dollar they received. They are not inclined to look kindly upon the move whereby the government says, "We know you investment people paid only 92 or 93 cents on the dollar but we will give you 100 cents on the dollar. What is more we will pay you a cash bonus and a commission for converting the bonds which you yourselves hold and what is even more we will give you a new bond by which you will be assured an interest rate from 4-J per cent over the next 25 years involving not only this generation but the next generation of taxpayers."
If ever there was a case of "To him who hath shall be given and from him who hath not shall be taken even that which he hath" this is it. The people of Canada who held these victory bonds and who hated to have to sell them at a discount a few years ago are going to remember this sell-out of the welfare of the common people, of Canada on the part of the Conservative government. The Canadian people remember the slogans, "Ward off inflation," "help win the war," "be patriotic," "save your money and do not buy a car or a house or washing machine or frigidaire that you need so badly".
Had the government of the day told us of the sell-out that would take place once the war and the immediate post-war period was over the Canadian people would have hesitated before investing their money in victory bonds. The rise in the interest rate surely was

In my view it speaks louder than any words of the Minister of Finance or of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) concerning where the allegiance of the Tory party lies.
